extracted.intended_audience: readers of exploration narratives and practical seafaring/exploration officers (19th-century explorers, naval officers, surveyors) and readers interested in naturalhistory/ethnography
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and descriptive guidance embedded in a 19th-century exploration/travel narrative: navigational notes, ethnographic observations, specimen-collection practice, and advice for future explorers. The page models how to record, name, and interpret discoveries while conducting coastal surveys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always assume natives carry arms nearby
rubrics_metrics.description: Speaking of natives appearing without spears, reminds me to mention for the information of future explorers, that their arms are always near at hand. They even trail them sometimes between their toes, a fact which travellers should ever bear in mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat apparent unarmed approach with caution: do not assume absence of weapons means no danger. Keep this in mind when approaching or landing; be prepared for concealed arms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make vocabularies only of words known to be correct
rubrics_metrics.description: Though, however, we may not attain to a knowledge of the truth at once, yet should we never lose an opportunity of making a vocabulary of such words as we know to be correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transient visitors often record incorrect meanings (many recorded 'names' are actually expressions like "I do not understand"). Verify words by repeated, careful inquiry and extended acquaintance; record only words you are confident about to avoid propagating errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inferring common linguistic roots from superficial likenesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Quote from Strzelecki: the inability of natives from different districts to understand one another shows dialects are far from possessing identities; seizing upon analogous words across districts without a thorough knowledge is premature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer common roots from a few similar-sounding words. Recognize syntactic ignorance and pronunciation/alphabet differences; comparative lexical claims require deep, systematic linguistic knowledge and long-term study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vegetation and birdlife as indicators of freshwater
rubrics_metrics.description: The green appearance of the gumtrees and an occasional clump of palms, which had pleasingly succeeded the mangroves, as they advanced, assured Captain Wickham that there was fresh water near. I inferred presence of a swamp from seeing the ibis flocking from the south-west up the south inlet in Port Darwin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When searching for freshwater in arid regions, look for green gumtrees, palms, flocks of ibis, and other vegetation/driftwood as reliable indicators of nearby freshwater or swampy ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document well construction, strata, and water behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: The water oozed through the sides, beginning to do so at a depth of twenty-five feet. The strata cut through varied considerably, in part consisting of ironstone mixed with a white kind of marl or pipeclay, for eight feet, then sandstone of a reddish colour ... remaining portion ... a sandy mud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record detailed strata descriptions (composition and depths) and note how and where water appears in wells. Precise geological notes help judge yield and permanence of water supplies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record precise latitudes and longitudes for observations
rubrics_metrics.description: The position of this well is in a small valley at the east end of the first sandy bay within Point Emery, in the centre of which the observations were made, placing it in latitude 12 degrees 27 minutes 45 seconds, longitude 1 degree 19 minutes 40 seconds, East of Port Essington.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give exact coordinates for wells, anchorage points, and other fixed observations to enable future visitors to locate features reliably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mark best anchorage and local hazards clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: The entrance points ... are white cliffy projections ... Just outside them lies a long four fathom bank ... The best anchorage is near Point Emery. Passing on the west side of the four fathom bank, where the channel is a mile wide and 10 fathoms deep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When charting a harbour: identify best anchorage, note shoals/banks and their depths, mark safe channels and where drying patches occur; provide leading marks and bearings to help navigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note limits of navigational guides and drying patches
rubrics_metrics.description: This guide is only, however, of service to a certain distance within the entrance, as it leads over a small patch that dries at low-water, distant two and a half miles ... To avoid this danger, it is therefore necessary to haul over towards Quail Island, when the highest hummock on it bears South-West 1/2 West.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state where marks/lines cease to be safe and give alternative bearings or manoeuvres to avoid drying patches and other hazards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record tidal behaviour and rates locally
rubrics_metrics.description: The tide is very irregular in Port Darwin, rising at springs 24 feet, and at neaps sometimes only two; its rate being from one and a half to three knots. The time of high-water at the full and change of moon, was half-past five ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give local tidal ranges, rates, and typical times for high water (spring/neap and relation to nearby ports) so future navigation and anchoring decisions can be made safely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared to use additional anchors during squalls
rubrics_metrics.description: We were compelled to pass the night ... a circumstance rendered disagreeable by the recurrence of another midnight squall ... so severe as to require the use of a second anchor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry and be ready to deploy extra anchors when working in squall-prone coasts; expect sudden squalls and plan anchoring scope accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use boats and soundings to find channels for the ship
rubrics_metrics.description: It was now necessary to find a channel for the ship, which I succeeded in doing ... after passing some distance along the eastern side of a long dry sandbank, we were obliged again to anchor, both boats signalizing a depth of only two fathoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advance cautiously with boats sounding ahead to locate deep-water channels; anchor when insufficient depth; use channels between islands and swashways revealed by soundings and landmarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of a substantial river or important inlet
rubrics_metrics.description: As we proceeded inwards, several beautiful medusae passed the ship, and our hopes were roused to the highest pitch by the muddy appearance of the water ... the lead gave a depth of eighteen and twenty fathoms, the velocity of the stream at the same time clearly showing how large a body of water was pouring through ... driftwood and many minor appearances ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat muddy water, abundant driftwood, high depths near the mouth, strong stream velocities, mangrove-fringed creeks, and freshwater signs as collective indicators of a major river entrance worth exploring and charting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect specimens and make colored drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: On this beach several unsuccessful hauls were made with the seine, though a few rare and curious fish were taken, which Lieutenant Emery added to his collection of coloured drawings of Australian fish; some of them will be found in the appendix to this volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When encountering new fauna, collect specimens where practicable and produce coloured illustrations for records and appendices. Specimens and art increase scientific and public value of the account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret natives' behaviour with nuance and patience
rubrics_metrics.description: Their astonishment at the size of the wells was highly amusing ... maternal affection was strong within them, and risking all to save their offspring ... the varied expressions and play of countenance, showed how strongly their feelings were at work within ... 'irru, irru' when frightened by cigar smoke ... in a few days they had forgotten their fright, and had returned to renew the friendly relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe and report native behaviour sensitively: do not reduce actions to caricature. Note signs of fear, friendliness (e.g., coming unarmed), maternal behavior, and how small novelties (fire, cigarette smoke) can frighten then be remedied by patience and interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name new geographic features descriptively or honorifically
rubrics_metrics.description: We named [places] Bynoe Harbour (after Mr. Bynoe), Quail Island (from that bird being found in great abundance), McAdam Range (in honour of Mr. McAdam) ... Victoria River (named for her most gracious majesty the Queen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use obvious local characteristics (flora, fauna, shape) or honour notable persons when assigning names; document the reason for the name to aid future identification and charts.
